claim: The cohesin ring complex is required for sister chromatid cohesion.
source: The cohesin ring complex is required for numerous chromosomal transactions including sister chromatid cohesion, DNA damage repair and transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established function of cohesin.

claim: The cohesin ring complex is required for DNA damage repair.
source: The cohesin ring complex is required for numerous chromosomal transactions including sister chromatid cohesion, DNA damage repair and transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established function of cohesin.

claim: The cohesin ring complex is required for transcriptional regulation.
source: The cohesin ring complex is required for numerous chromosomal transactions including sister chromatid cohesion, DNA damage repair and transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established function of cohesin.

claim: Scc3 and Scc1 form a composite DNA interaction module.
source: We show here, by determining a crystal structure of the budding yeast cohesin HEAT-repeat subunit Scc3 bound to a fragment of the Scc1 kleisin subunit and DNA, that Scc3 and Scc1 form a composite DNA interaction module.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the crystal structure determination presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Scc3-Scc1 subcomplex engages double-stranded DNA through a conserved, positively charged surface.
source: The Scc3-Scc1 subcomplex engages double-stranded DNA through a conserved, positively charged surface.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and electrostatic surface analysis shown in the manuscript.

claim: The conserved DNA-binding domain of Scc3-Scc1 is required for DNA binding in vitro.
source: We demonstrate that this conserved domain is required for DNA binding by Scc3-Scc1 in vitro, as well as for the enrichment of cohesin on chromosomes and for cell viability.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mutagenesis and fluorescence polarization experiments.

claim: The conserved DNA-binding domain of Scc3-Scc1 is required for the enrichment of cohesin on chromosomes.
source: We demonstrate that this conserved domain is required for DNA binding by Scc3-Scc1 in vitro, as well as for the enrichment of cohesin on chromosomes and for cell viability.
evidence: This is demonstrated through ChIP-qPCR experiments with mutant variants.

claim: The conserved DNA-binding domain of Scc3-Scc1 is required for cell viability.
source: We demonstrate that this conserved domain is required for DNA binding by Scc3-Scc1 in vitro, as well as for the enrichment of cohesin on chromosomes and for cell viability.
evidence: This is demonstrated through tetrad analysis showing that heptamutant cells fail to divide.

claim: The Scc3-Scc1 DNA-binding interface plays a central role in the recruitment of cohesin complexes to chromosomes.
source: These findings suggest that the Scc3-Scc1 DNA-binding interface plays a central role in the recruitment of cohesin complexes to chromosomes and therefore for cohesin to faithfully execute its functions during cell division.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of in vitro DNA binding, ChIP-qPCR, and viability assays.

claim: Cognate chromatids are paired through replication-coupled sister chromatid cohesion.
source: To ensure that each daughter cell receives an equal complement of genetic information, cognate chromatids are paired through replication-coupled sister chromatid cohesion.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of chromosome biology.

claim: Cohesion enables attachment of kinetochores to the mitotic spindle microtubules emanating from opposite poles to ensure chromosome bi-orientation.
source: Cohesion is then actively maintained and eventually enables attachment of kinetochores to the mitotic spindle microtubules emanating from opposite poles to ensure chromosome bi-orientation, prior to subsequent segregation of sister chromatids into daughter cells (Nasmyth and Haering, 2009; Peters and Nishiyama, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Cohesion is facilitated by cohesin, a member of the Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes (SMC) family of protein complexes.
source: Cohesion is facilitated by cohesin, a member of the Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes (SMC) family of protein complexes, which is responsible for genome organisation across all domains of life (Palecek and Gruber, 2015; Wells et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Cohesin complexes form tripartite rings, comprising Smc1-Smc3 and the kleisin subunit Scc1.
source: Cohesin complexes form tripartite rings, comprising Smc1-Smc3 and the kleisin subunit Scc1, that are proposed to topologically entrap sister DNA molecules (Gligoris et al., 2014; Nasmyth and Haering, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Cohesin rings are proposed to topologically entrap sister DNA molecules.
source: Cohesin complexes form tripartite rings, comprising Smc1-Smc3 and the kleisin subunit Scc1, that are proposed to topologically entrap sister DNA molecules (Gligoris et al., 2014; Nasmyth and Haering, 2009).
evidence: This is a model supported by cited references.

claim: The chromosomal addresses of cohesin loading are determined by the Scc2-Scc4 complex.
source: The chromosomal addresses of cohesin loading are determined by the Scc2-Scc4 complex, which is enriched at centromeres via direct contacts with kinetochore proteins and promotes DNA-stimulated ATP hydrolysis by the Smc1-Smc3 ATPase heads to drive chromatin entrapment (Ciosk et al., 2000; Hinshaw et al., 2017; Murayama and Uhlmann, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: The Scc2-Scc4 complex is enriched at centromeres via direct contacts with kinetochore proteins.
source: The chromosomal addresses of cohesin loading are determined by the Scc2-Scc4 complex, which is enriched at centromeres via direct contacts with kinetochore proteins and promotes DNA-stimulated ATP hydrolysis by the Smc1-Smc3 ATPase heads to drive chromatin entrapment (Ciosk et al., 2000; Hinshaw et al., 2017; Murayama and Uhlmann, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: The Scc2-Scc4 complex promotes DNA-stimulated ATP hydrolysis by the Smc1-Smc3 ATPase heads to drive chromatin entrapment.
source: The chromosomal addresses of cohesin loading are determined by the Scc2-Scc4 complex, which is enriched at centromeres via direct contacts with kinetochore proteins and promotes DNA-stimulated ATP hydrolysis by the Smc1-Smc3 ATPase heads to drive chromatin entrapment (Ciosk et al., 2000; Hinshaw et al., 2017; Murayama and Uhlmann, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Dynamic release of DNA from the cohesin ring is achieved by the proteolytic cleavage of the Scc1 kleisin subunit by separase protease.
source: Conversely, dynamic release of DNA from the ring is achieved either by the proteolytic cleavage of the Scc1 kleisin subunit by separase protease (Uhlmann et al., 2000), or by the opening of an 'exit gate' formed at the Scc1 and Smc3 interface.
evidence: This is supported by cited reference.

claim: Dynamic release of DNA from the cohesin ring is achieved by the opening of an 'exit gate' formed at the Scc1 and Smc3 interface.
source: Conversely, dynamic release of DNA from the ring is achieved either by the proteolytic cleavage of the Scc1 kleisin subunit by separase protease (Uhlmann et al., 2000), or by the opening of an 'exit gate' formed at the Scc1 and Smc3 interface.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Release of the exit gate is inhibited by Smc3 acetylation.
source: Release of the latter is inhibited by Smc3 acetylation and is controlled by the accessory factors Scc3, Wapl and Pds5 (Beckouët et al., 2016; Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2008; Rowland et al., 2009; Unal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Release of the exit gate is controlled by the accessory factors Scc3, Wapl and Pds5.
source: Release of the latter is inhibited by Smc3 acetylation and is controlled by the accessory factors Scc3, Wapl and Pds5 (Beckouët et al., 2016; Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2008; Rowland et al., 2009; Unal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Cohesin can associate dynamically with chromatin through alternating cycles of DNA entrapment and release until ring opening is inhibited by acetylation of the Smc3 ATPase head.
source: Cohesin can associate dynamically with chromatin through alternating cycles of DNA entrapment and release until ring opening is inhibited by acetylation of the Smc3 ATPase head.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: DNA is thought to remain topologically entrapped within the SMC-kleisin ring after ring opening is inhibited by Smc3 acetylation.
source: At this point, DNA is thought to remain topologically entrapped within the SMC-kleisin ring (Gligoris et al., 2014; Beckouët et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a model supported by cited references.

claim: A prevailing model of genome organisation posits that chromatin loops entrapped within the lumen of the SMC ring are processively enlarged by extrusion.
source: A prevailing model of genome organisation posits that chromatin loops entrapped within the lumen of the SMC ring are then processively enlarged by extrusion, which presumably forms the basis for higher-order chromatin structure (Alipour and Marko, 2012).
evidence: This is a model supported by cited reference.

claim: The essential role of cohesin in modulating genome architecture is increasingly well established.
source: Whereas the essential role of cohesin in modulating genome architecture, gene expression and DNA damage repair is increasingly well established, comparatively little information is available concerning the molecular determinants of its association with chromatin (Busslinger et al., 2017; Haarhuis et al., 2017; Schwarzer et al., 2017; Wu and Yu, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: The essential role of cohesin in gene expression is increasingly well established.
source: Whereas the essential role of cohesin in modulating genome architecture, gene expression and DNA damage repair is increasingly well established, comparatively little information is available concerning the molecular determinants of its association with chromatin (Busslinger et al., 2017; Haarhuis et al., 2017; Schwarzer et al., 2017; Wu and Yu, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Comparatively little information is available concerning the molecular determinants of cohesin's association with chromatin.
source: Whereas the essential role of cohesin in modulating genome architecture, gene expression and DNA damage repair is increasingly well established, comparatively little information is available concerning the molecular determinants of its association with chromatin (Busslinger et al., 2017; Haarhuis et al., 2017; Schwarzer et al., 2017; Wu and Yu, 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by cited references.

claim: Recent work identified a direct DNA-binding site in the paralogous condensin complex.
source: Recent work identified a direct DNA-binding site in the paralogous condensin complex, in which the HEAT repeat subunit Ycg1, in complex with the kleisin subunit Brn1, contacts the DNA double helix backbone and stabilizes its association through DNA entrapment within the Brn1 peptide loop (Kschonsak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited reference.

claim: In condensin, the HEAT repeat subunit Ycg1, in complex with the kleisin subunit Brn1, contacts the DNA double helix backbone.
source: Recent work identified a direct DNA-binding site in the paralogous condensin complex, in which the HEAT repeat subunit Ycg1, in complex with the kleisin subunit Brn1, contacts the DNA double helix backbone and stabilizes its association through DNA entrapment within the Brn1 peptide loop (Kschonsak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited reference.

claim: In condensin, DNA association is stabilized through DNA entrapment within the Brn1 peptide loop.
source: Recent work identified a direct DNA-binding site in the paralogous condensin complex, in which the HEAT repeat subunit Ycg1, in complex with the kleisin subunit Brn1, contacts the DNA double helix backbone and stabilizes its association through DNA entrapment within the Brn1 peptide loop (Kschonsak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited reference.

claim: The essential HEAT-repeat subunit Scc3, when in complex with Scc1, binds double-stranded DNA (dsDNA).
source: We found that the essential HEAT-repeat subunit Scc3, when in complex with Scc1, binds double-stranded DNA (dsDNA).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by EMSA experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: DNA binding by the Scc3-Scc1 complex is mediated by a composite surface comprising positively charged amino acid residues from Scc3 and Scc1.
source: We further determined the crystal structure of the yeast Scc3-Scc1 complex bound to DNA, which revealed that DNA binding is mediated by a composite surface comprising positively charged amino acid residues from Scc3 and Scc1.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and electrostatic surface analysis.

claim: Direct DNA substrate engagement through the DNA-binding interface of the Scc3-Scc1 subcomplex is a key element for the cohesin cycle.
source: Thus, direct DNA substrate engagement through the newly discovered DNA-binding interface of the Scc3-Scc1 subcomplex is a key element for the cohesin cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of structural, biochemical, and cell biological experiments.

claim: The Smc3hd-NScc1 module binds DNA.
source: Consistent with prior studies (Murayama and Uhlmann, 2014), we found that the Scc3T-Scc1K subcomplex and the Smc1-Smc3 hinge heterodimer bound DNA, as seen by the appearance of slower-migrating species in electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSAs), as did the Smc3hd-NScc1 module, which has previously been implicated as a DNA sensor in cohesin (Murayama and Uhlmann, 2014) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Smc1-Smc3 hinge heterodimer binds DNA.
source: Consistent with prior studies (Murayama and Uhlmann, 2014), we found that the Scc3T-Scc1K subcomplex and the Smc1-Smc3 hinge heterodimer bound DNA, as seen by the appearance of slower-migrating species in electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSAs), as did the Smc3hd-NScc1 module, which has previously been implicated as a DNA sensor in cohesin (Murayama and Uhlmann, 2014) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Scc3T-Scc1K subcomplex binds DNA.
source: Consistent with prior studies (Murayama and Uhlmann, 2014), we found that the Scc3T-Scc1K subcomplex and the Smc1-Smc3 hinge heterodimer bound DNA, as seen by the appearance of slower-migrating species in electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSAs), as did the Smc3hd-NScc1 module, which has previously been implicated as a DNA sensor in cohesin (Murayama and Uhlmann, 2014) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Longer DNA fragments (>21 base pairs) bind more efficiently to cohesin subcomplexes than shorter DNA duplexes (15 bp).
source: As expected for non-sequence specific DNA-binding factors, longer DNA fragments (>21 base pairs (bp)) bound more efficiently than shorter DNA duplexes (15 bp) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ability of the Scc3T-Scc1K subcomplex to bind DNA depends on the presence of Scc1K.
source: The ability of the Scc3T-Scc1K subcomplex to bind DNA depended on the presence of Scc1K.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA experiments comparing Scc3T alone versus Scc3T-Scc1K complex.

claim: The Pds5-Scc1 subcomplex does not interact with DNA.
source: Conversely, the other HEAT-repeat-kleisin subcomplex of cohesin, Pds5-Scc1, the Smc1hd-CScc1 subcomplex and the Wapl subunit did not interact with DNA in this assay.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: The Smc1hd-CScc1 subcomplex does not interact with DNA.
source: Conversely, the other HEAT-repeat-kleisin subcomplex of cohesin, Pds5-Scc1, the Smc1hd-CScc1 subcomplex and the Wapl subunit did not interact with DNA in this assay.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: The Wapl subunit does not interact with DNA.
source: Conversely, the other HEAT-repeat-kleisin subcomplex of cohesin, Pds5-Scc1, the Smc1hd-CScc1 subcomplex and the Wapl subunit did not interact with DNA in this assay.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: As in the paralogous condensin complex, the HEAT-repeat protein bound to the C-terminal region of the kleisin subunit directly engages DNA.
source: Thus, as in the paralogous condensin complex, the HEAT-repeat protein bound to the C-terminal region of the kleisin subunit directly engages DNA (Kschonsak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of cohesin and condensin DNA-binding properties, supported by cited reference.

claim: Optimized crystals of the Scc3T-Scc1K complex bound to 19 bp dsDNA diffracted anisotropically to a minimum Bragg spacing of 3.6 Å in the best direction.
source: Optimized crystals diffracted anisotropically to a minimum Bragg spacing of 3.6 Å in the best, and ~5.7 Å in the worst direction (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from X-ray crystallography experiments.

claim: Optimized crystals of the Scc3T-Scc1K complex bound to 19 bp dsDNA diffracted anisotropically to ~5.7 Å in the worst direction.
source: Optimized crystals diffracted anisotropically to a minimum Bragg spacing of 3.6 Å in the best, and ~5.7 Å in the worst direction (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from X-ray crystallography experiments.

claim: The structure of the Scc3T-Scc1K-DNA complex was determined by molecular replacement using structures of Scc3 orthologs as search models.
source: We determined the structure by molecular replacement, using the structures of an Scc3 ortholog from Zygosaccharomyces rouxii and a C-terminal fragment of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Scc3 as search models (Roig et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the method used for structure determination, supported by cited reference.

claim: The refined model of the Scc3T-Scc1K-DNA complex encompasses amino acid residues 134 to 1064 of Scc3.
source: Despite these drawbacks, we successfully traced the structure using a selenomethionine derivative and refined a model encompassing amino acid residues 134 to 1064 of Scc3 in complex with residues 309 to 400 of Scc1, bound to a 19 bp DNA molecule (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from the structure determination.

claim: The refined model of the Scc3T-Scc1K-DNA complex encompasses residues 309 to 400 of Scc1.
source: Despite these drawbacks, we successfully traced the structure using a selenomethionine derivative and refined a model encompassing amino acid residues 134 to 1064 of Scc3 in complex with residues 309 to 400 of Scc1, bound to a 19 bp DNA molecule (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from the structure determination.

claim: The refined model of the Scc3T-Scc1K-DNA complex includes a 19 bp DNA molecule.
source: Despite these drawbacks, we successfully traced the structure using a selenomethionine derivative and refined a model encompassing amino acid residues 134 to 1064 of Scc3 in complex with residues 309 to 400 of Scc1, bound to a 19 bp DNA molecule (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from the structure determination.

claim: Scc3 is hook-shaped in the C-terminal section.
source: As seen in other structures of Scc3, the protein is hook-shaped in the C-terminal section and contains an N-terminal 'nose' formed by a pair of extended antiparallel α-helices (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Scc3 contains an N-terminal 'nose' formed by a pair of extended antiparallel α-helices.
source: As seen in other structures of Scc3, the protein is hook-shaped in the C-terminal section and contains an N-terminal 'nose' formed by a pair of extended antiparallel α-helices (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Yeast Scc1 binds along the convex surface of the hook-shaped HEAT-repeat subunit Scc3.
source: Similarly to the interaction of human Scc1 with Scc3, the yeast Scc1 in our structure binds along the convex surface of the hook-shaped HEAT-repeat subunit.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: dsDNA is located within the cradle of the hook-shaped Scc3 structure.
source: We detected additional electron density corresponding to dsDNA within the cradle of this hook (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is observed in the electron density maps shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: DNA duplexes aligned to form pseudocontinuous double helices throughout the crystal.
source: Whereas the DNA duplexes aligned to form pseudocontinuous double helices throughout the crystal, the DNA duplex was slightly too short for tight end-to-end stacking (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The DNA duplex was slightly too short for tight end-to-end stacking in the crystal.
source: Whereas the DNA duplexes aligned to form pseudocontinuous double helices throughout the crystal, the DNA duplex was slightly too short for tight end-to-end stacking (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The DNA density was only partially resolved due to rotational and translational disorder of the DNA in the binding cavity.
source: As a result, the DNA density was only partially resolved, apparently due to rotational and translational disorder of the DNA in the binding cavity.
evidence: This is inferred from the quality of the electron density maps.

claim: DNA is nested within an extended cradle spanning the majority of Scc3-Scc1, lined by a set of positively charged residues that directly contact the DNA phosphate backbone.
source: This revealed that DNA is nested within an extended cradle spanning the majority of Scc3-Scc1, lined by a set of positively charged residues that directly contact the DNA phosphate backbone.
evidence: This is observed from the electrostatic surface potential mapping and crystal structure.

claim: The DNA is aligned almost parallel to the N-terminal 'nose' of Scc3.
source: The DNA is aligned almost parallel to the N-terminal 'nose' of Scc3, which interacts through a set of positively charged amino acid residues with the DNA of a neighbouring complex related by crystallographic symmetry (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The N-terminal 'nose' of Scc3 interacts through a set of positively charged amino acid residues with the DNA of a neighbouring complex related by crystallographic symmetry.
source: The DNA is aligned almost parallel to the N-terminal 'nose' of Scc3, which interacts through a set of positively charged amino acid residues with the DNA of a neighbouring complex related by crystallographic symmetry (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No direct nucleotide base–amino acid interactions were observed in the Scc3-Scc1-DNA structure.
source: We observed no direct nucleotide base–amino acid interactions, which explains the apparent lack of DNA sequence specificity.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The lack of direct nucleotide base–amino acid interactions explains the apparent lack of DNA sequence specificity of Scc3-Scc1.
source: We observed no direct nucleotide base–amino acid interactions, which explains the apparent lack of DNA sequence specificity.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: An anomalous difference map peak for M373 in the selenomethionine-derivative data was used to ascertain the amino-acid register of Scc1.
source: To ascertain the amino-acid register of Scc1, we used an anomalous difference map peak for M373 in the selenomethionine-derivative data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a method used in structure determination, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The deduced register places Scc1 residue K363 in close proximity to the DNA.
source: The deduced register places Scc1 residue K363 in close proximity to the DNA (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Direct interactions between Scc1 and the DNA phosphate backbone potentially explain why the Scc3T-Scc1K subcomplex has greater DNA binding affinity than isolated Scc3T.
source: Direct interactions between Scc1 and the DNA phosphate backbone potentially explain why the Scc3T-Scc1K subcomplex has greater DNA binding affinity than does isolated Scc3T (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and EMSA data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Amino acid residues in the DNA binding groove of Scc3 are generally well conserved among yeast Scc3 orthologs.
source: Mapping of sequence conservation onto the structure revealed that amino acid residues in the DNA binding groove are generally well conserved among yeast Scc3 orthologs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by sequence conservation analysis displayed in Figure 3A.

claim: Amino acid residues located proximal to the DNA phosphate backbone in Scc3 show strong conservation.
source: In particular, amino acid residues that are located proximal to the DNA phosphate backbone showed strong conservation.
evidence: This is shown by sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The wild-type Scc3T-Scc1K complex binds a 32-bp 6-FAM labelled DNA substrate with an equilibrium dissociation constant of 2.2 μM.
source: Whereas the wild-type Scc3T-Scc1K complex bound this substrate with an equilibrium dissociation constant of 2.2 μM, charge-inversion mutations in patches 1 and 3, located at the crest of and within the Scc3 cradle, had only modest effects on affinity (equilibrium dissociation constants of 9.5 μM and 7.3 μM, respectively).
evidence: This is measured by fluorescence polarization experiments.

claim: Charge-inversion mutations in patch 1 of Scc3 result in an equilibrium dissociation constant of 9.5 μM for DNA binding.
source: Whereas the wild-type Scc3T-Scc1K complex bound this substrate with an equilibrium dissociation constant of 2.2 μM, charge-inversion mutations in patches 1 and 3, located at the crest of and within the Scc3 cradle, had only modest effects on affinity (equilibrium dissociation constants of 9.5 μM and 7.3 μM, respectively).
evidence: This is measured by fluorescence polarization experiments.

claim: Charge-inversion mutations in patch 3 of Scc3 result in an equilibrium dissociation constant of 7.3 μM for DNA binding.
source: Whereas the wild-type Scc3T-Scc1K complex bound this substrate with an equilibrium dissociation constant of 2.2 μM, charge-inversion mutations in patches 1 and 3, located at the crest of and within the Scc3 cradle, had only modest effects on affinity (equilibrium dissociation constants of 9.5 μM and 7.3 μM, respectively).
evidence: This is measured by fluorescence polarization experiments.

claim: Patch 2 mutants of Scc3 exhibit essentially unaltered DNA binding affinity.
source: Patch 2 mutants, residing in the Scc3 'nose', exhibited essentially unaltered DNA binding affinity.
evidence: This is measured by fluorescence polarization experiments.

claim: The simultaneous mutation of all three patches in Scc3 (heptamutant) reduces the binding affinity to 29.3 μM.
source: In contrast, the simultaneous mutation of all three patches (a heptamutant) reduced the binding affinity of the patch 1 or 3 mutants even further (to 29.3 μM, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is measured by fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The defect in DNA binding by Scc3 mutants was not due to any impact of the mutations on the structural integrity of Scc3-Scc1.
source: The defect in binding DNA was not due to any impact of the mutations on the structural integrity of Scc3-Scc1, as all mutant complexes eluted indistinguishably from wild-type Scc3-Scc1 during size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and efficiently formed a complex with Scc1 in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) or in vivo (see below).
evidence: This is supported by size-exclusion chromatography shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and SDS-PAGE shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All mutant Scc3-Scc1 complexes eluted indistinguishably from wild-type Scc3-Scc1 during size-exclusion chromatography.
source: The defect in binding DNA was not due to any impact of the mutations on the structural integrity of Scc3-Scc1, as all mutant complexes eluted indistinguishably from wild-type Scc3-Scc1 during size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and efficiently formed a complex with Scc1 in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) or in vivo (see below).
evidence: This is shown by size-exclusion chromatography in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All mutant Scc3 variants efficiently formed a complex with Scc1 in vitro.
source: The defect in binding DNA was not due to any impact of the mutations on the structural integrity of Scc3-Scc1, as all mutant complexes eluted indistinguishably from wild-type Scc3-Scc1 during size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and efficiently formed a complex with Scc1 in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) or in vivo (see below).
evidence: This is shown by SDS-PAGE in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The positively charged Scc3 cradle comprises the major DNA-binding surface of Scc3.
source: We conclude that the positively charged Scc3 cradle comprises the major DNA-binding surface of Scc3 and that the positively charged amino acid residues located in patch 1 and 3 constitute a composite DNA binding surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis and DNA binding experiments.

claim: The positively charged amino acid residues located in patch 1 and 3 of Scc3 constitute a composite DNA binding surface.
source: We conclude that the positively charged Scc3 cradle comprises the major DNA-binding surface of Scc3 and that the positively charged amino acid residues located in patch 1 and 3 constitute a composite DNA binding surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis and DNA binding experiments.

claim: The K363E/R364E double mutation in Scc1K shows an essentially indistinguishable equilibrium dissociation constant compared to the wild-type complex.
source: To test whether the direct interactions between Scc1 and the DNA phosphate backbone contribute to DNA binding we introduced the double mutation K363E/R364E into Scc1K. This mutant showed an essentially indistinguishable equilibrium dissociation constant as compared to that of the wild-type complex, thus indicating that this positively charged patch of Scc1 does not contribute to DNA binding (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is measured by fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The positively charged patch K363/R364 of Scc1 does not contribute to DNA binding.
source: To test whether the direct interactions between Scc1 and the DNA phosphate backbone contribute to DNA binding we introduced the double mutation K363E/R364E into Scc1K. This mutant showed an essentially indistinguishable equilibrium dissociation constant as compared to that of the wild-type complex, thus indicating that this positively charged patch of Scc1 does not contribute to DNA binding (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from the fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All three individual patch mutants of Scc3 can support cell proliferation.
source: Whereas all three individual patch mutants could support cell proliferation, cells expressing the heptamutant mutant version as their only source of Scc3 failed to divide, despite expressing the mutant Scc3 protein at wild-type levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown by tetrad dissection experiments.

claim: Cells expressing the heptamutant version of Scc3 as their only source of Scc3 fail to divide.
source: Whereas all three individual patch mutants could support cell proliferation, cells expressing the heptamutant mutant version as their only source of Scc3 failed to divide, despite expressing the mutant Scc3 protein at wild-type levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown by tetrad dissection experiments in Figure 3D.

claim: The heptamutant Scc3 protein is expressed at wild-type levels.
source: Whereas all three individual patch mutants could support cell proliferation, cells expressing the heptamutant mutant version as their only source of Scc3 failed to divide, despite expressing the mutant Scc3 protein at wild-type levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown by western blotting in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The findings provide evidence for a site of direct DNA contact in cohesin complexes.

These findings provide evidence for a site of direct DNA contact in cohesin complexes, which presumably contributes to the initial step of chromosome entrapment and/or DNA translocation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Direct DNA-cohesin interactions likely contribute to DNA entry and exit reactions.
